\chapter{Excuse Me, and Say It Again}
\label{ch:ru-repair}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in both the light and the heavy way, open a request to a stranger, ask for a repeat, ask somebody to speak slowly, and ask for help.}

The track could say ya ne ponimayu and ya ne znayu in full and had no word for sorry, no way to ask for a repeat and no way to open a request to a stranger: it could report a failure and do nothing about it. Five words close that. The chapter also names the -ite ending, which turns three words the reader would otherwise memorise separately into one set -- and the last of the five, pomogite, is built entirely out of parts the reader already had.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[izvinítye]{\ru{извините} — the word the book has been missing since page one}

\label{lesson:RU-C21-izvinite}



\begin{quote}
The two courtesy words you have had since the first chapter, and a verb.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{понимать}}, on a root meaning \textbf{to take hold of}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{спасибо}}, and \emph{\ru{чтобы}} with an infinitive after it
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{но}}, the contradicting \emph{but} with no secure English cousin
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{надо}} with nobody in the sentence, and \emph{\ru{хотеть}}, which has no cousin outside Slavic
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{извините}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{извините}} — \emph{izvinítye} — \textbf{excuse me, sorry}
\end{itemize}

Four syllables, stress on the third: \emph{iz-vi-NÍ-tye}. It is the single most useful word left in this book, and it does two separate jobs:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{an apology}, when you have got something wrong
  \item \textbf{an opening}, when you want to speak to somebody you do not know
\end{itemize}

The second is the one to notice. A Russian does not walk up to a stranger and start; they say \textbf{\ru{извините}} first, every time. It is the equivalent of \emph{excuse me} at the front of a question, and without it the question can sound abrupt in a way you did not intend.

The ending \textbf{-\ru{ите}} is the polite one, the same \textbf{\ru{вы}} that \textbf{\ru{здравствуйте}} carries. Said to a friend it would be \textbf{\ru{извини}}, without the \textbf{\ru{те}} — but reach for the long one by default, exactly as you do with the greeting.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{извините}} is \textbf{\ru{из}-} (\textquotedblleft{}out of\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\ru{вина}} (\textquotedblleft{}guilt, fault\textquotedblright{}), with the polite ending on the end.

So the word literally asks the other person to take you \textbf{out of the blame} — which is a real picture, still visible in the Russian, and one English threw away when \emph{excuse} stopped meaning anything at all on its own.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{извините}} — \emph{iz-vi-NÍ-tye}, stress on the third
  \item \emph{\ru{извините}, \ru{пожалуйста}} — the two courtesy words together
  \item it as an opening, before anything else you know how to ask
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}excuse me.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{извините}}.) Name its two jobs. (\textbf{An apology}, and \textbf{the opening of a request to a stranger}.) What does it literally ask for? (\textbf{To be taken out of the guilt}.) And one look back: what does \emph{\ru{понимать}} literally do? (\textbf{Takes hold}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prastítye]{\ru{простите} — the heavier apology}

\label{lesson:RU-C21-prostite}



\begin{quote}
Yesterday's word, and a verb from long before it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{читать}}, which sits with the words for \textbf{honour} and \textbf{number} on a root meaning \emph{to count, to heed}
  \item \emph{Recall:} that Russian has no separate \emph{I am reading}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{извините}}, and \emph{\ru{хотеть}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{а}}, the \emph{whereas} word, and the test that tells it from \emph{\ru{но}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{простите}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{простите}} — \emph{prastítye} — \textbf{forgive me}
\end{itemize}

Same shape as yesterday's word, same polite \textbf{-\ru{ите}} ending, and the informal \textbf{\ru{прости}} sitting behind it in exactly the same way.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{извините}} asks to be \textbf{let off}
  \item \textbf{\ru{простите}} asks to be \textbf{forgiven}
\end{itemize}

Both come out as \emph{sorry} in English and they are not interchangeable in Russian.

\begin{culture}
What separates them is \textbf{weight}, not politeness — both words are polite.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{извините}} for the small thing: bumping somebody, interrupting, opening a request to a stranger. Nobody is really being blamed.
  \item \textbf{\ru{простите}} for the real one: you have let somebody down and you are asking them to release you from it.
\end{itemize}

Use \textbf{\ru{простите}} for a trodden foot and you sound as though you had wrecked their week. Use \textbf{\ru{извините}} after a genuine wrong and you sound as though it did not matter.

This is the same pair-with-a-rule that \textbf{\ru{здравствуйте}} and \emph{\ru{привет}} form for greetings — Russian keeps a formal and a casual option side by side and expects you to choose. The difference here is that the choice is about the size of the offence rather than about who you are talking to.

The etymology carries the same weight: \textbf{\ru{простите}} is built on \textbf{\ru{простой}}, \emph{simple, straight} — to forgive is to make something straight again.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{простите}} — \emph{pras-TÍ-tye}
  \item \emph{Say it:} both words in turn, and say what each is for
  \item \emph{Build:} pick the right one for stepping on a foot, and for missing a meeting
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two is the heavier apology? (That is \textbf{\ru{простите}}.) What separates the two? (\textbf{The size of the offence}, not politeness.) What does the root of \textbf{\ru{простите}} mean? (\textbf{Simple, straight} — to forgive is to make straight.) And one look back: which greeting is the formal one? (That is \textbf{\ru{здравствуйте}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paftarítye]{\ru{повторите} — asking for it again}

\label{lesson:RU-C21-povtorite}



\begin{quote}
A verb from the hand chapter, and yesterday's apology.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{писать}}, on a root meaning \textbf{to scratch} — the same root as \emph{paint} — and the letter \textbf{\ru{ш}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} a bare infinitive after \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу}}, with nothing in between
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{простите}}, the heavier of the two apologies
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{один}}, whose root became English \emph{one}, \emph{an}, \emph{a}, \emph{alone} and \emph{only}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{чтобы}}, the purpose word built from \textbf{\ru{что}} plus \textbf{\ru{бы}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{повторите}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{повторите}} — \emph{paftarítye} — \textbf{say it again, repeat it}
\end{itemize}

Until now the book could report a failure and do nothing about it. \emph{\ru{Я} \ru{не} \ru{понимаю}} said something had gone wrong; it did not ask anybody to change anything. This word does.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{извините}, \ru{повторите}, \ru{пожалуйста}} — \emph{izvinítye, paftarítye, pazhálusta} — sorry, please say that again.
\end{itemize}

Three words you own, in the order a Russian says them: the opening, the request, the politeness. That is a complete repair turn.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the -\ru{ите} ending is an order}]
Three words in two lessons now end in \textbf{-\ru{ите}}: \textbf{\ru{извините}}, \textbf{\ru{простите}}, \textbf{\ru{повторите}}. That is not a coincidence and it is worth naming.

\textbf{-\ru{ите}} is Russian's polite \textbf{imperative} — the ending that turns a verb into an instruction addressed to \textbf{\ru{вы}}. Drop the \textbf{-\ru{те}} and you get the \textbf{\ru{ты}} form: \emph{\ru{извини}}, \emph{\ru{прости}}, \emph{\ru{повтори}}.

So the two apologies were never nouns. They were commands all along, and seeing the ending makes them a set instead of three things to memorise.

The word itself is \textbf{\ru{по}-} plus \textbf{\ru{втор}-}, \emph{second} — the same \textbf{\ru{втор}-} in \textbf{\ru{вторник}}, Tuesday, the second day. To repeat is to do a thing a second time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{повторите}, \ru{пожалуйста}}
  \item the whole turn — \emph{\ru{извините}, \ru{повторите}, \ru{пожалуйста}}
  \item the three \textbf{-\ru{ите}} words in a row, and hear the ending they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask somebody to say it again, politely. (That is \textbf{\ru{повторите}, \ru{пожалуйста}}.) What does the ending \textbf{-\ru{ите}} do? (\textbf{Turns a verb into a polite instruction} addressed to \emph{\ru{вы}}.) Which day of the week shares a piece with this word? (The day is \textbf{\ru{вторник}}, Tuesday, the second day.) And one look back: which letter did \emph{\ru{писать}} teach you? (That is \textbf{\ru{ш}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[myédlenna]{\ru{медленно} — asking for it slower}

\label{lesson:RU-C21-medlenno}



\begin{quote}
A verb from the hand chapter, and the divider from earlier.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{брать}}, English \emph{bear}, whose partner verb comes from a completely different root
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{другой}}, the split \emph{\ru{один} … \ru{другой} …}, and \emph{\ru{повторите}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{медленно}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{медленно}} — \emph{myédlenna} — \textbf{slowly}
\end{itemize}

Stress the first syllable, and let the two unstressed \textbf{\ru{о}} and \textbf{\ru{е}} at the end soften: \emph{MYÉD-len-na}.

Its shape is worth a moment. Russian makes an adverb by putting \textbf{-\ru{о}} on the end of a describing word, and that is the whole rule — no ending to agree with anything, nothing to change. It is the simplest piece of grammar in this chapter and one of the most productive in the language.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the second repair move}]
Take \textbf{\ru{говорить}}, put the polite \textbf{-\ru{ите}} on it, and add the adverb:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{говорите} \ru{медленно}, \ru{пожалуйста}} — \emph{gavarítye myédlenna, pazhálusta} — please speak slowly.
\end{itemize}

That is a genuinely different move from \textbf{\ru{повторите}}. Asking for a repeat gets you the same sentence at the same speed; asking for \textbf{\ru{медленно}} changes what the other person is doing. A listener who owns both can steer a conversation instead of only reporting on it.

The repair kit is now complete, and it is four words long: \textbf{\ru{извините}}, \textbf{\ru{повторите}}, \textbf{\ru{говорите} \ru{медленно}}, \textbf{\ru{пожалуйста}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{медленно}} — \emph{MYÉD-len-na}
  \item \emph{\ru{говорите} \ru{медленно}, \ru{пожалуйста}}
  \item the whole kit in order — sorry, again, slower, please
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask somebody to speak slowly. (That is \textbf{\ru{говорите} \ru{медленно}, \ru{пожалуйста}}.) How does Russian make an adverb? (\textbf{By putting -\ru{о} on the end}.) What does asking for \textbf{\ru{медленно}} get you that a repeat does not? (\textbf{A change in what the speaker is doing}, not the same sentence again.) And one look back: which verb means \emph{to take}? (That is \textbf{\ru{брать}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pamagítye]{\ru{помогите} — the request you already knew how to make}

\label{lesson:RU-C21-pomogite}



\begin{quote}
The asking verb, and yesterday's adverb.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{спрашивать}}, on the root that gave Latin its word for \textbf{pray}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{говорите} \ru{медленно}}, and \emph{\ru{тоже}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the dot on the line, and the single question mark at the end
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{помогите}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{помогите}} — \emph{pamagítye} — \textbf{help me}
\end{itemize}

There is almost nothing new in this word, and that is the point of putting it here. You have had \textbf{\ru{помогать}} since the verbs of the hand. You learned \textbf{-\ru{ите}} two lessons ago. Put them together and you have the most important single word in any emergency, built entirely out of parts you owned already.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{извините}, \ru{помогите}, \ru{пожалуйста}} — \emph{izvinítye, pamagítye, pazhálusta} — excuse me, please help.
\end{itemize}

Say it once out loud. A course that can greet, thank, apologise, ask for a repeat, ask for slower speech and ask for help has covered every move a beginner needs to survive a conversation that goes wrong — and every one of those moves arrived in this chapter or the ones just behind it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{помогите}} — \emph{pa-ma-GÍ-tye}
  \item \emph{\ru{извините}, \ru{помогите}, \ru{пожалуйста}}
  \item the four -\ru{ите} words together — excuse, forgive, repeat, help
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for help, politely and completely. (That is \textbf{\ru{извините}, \ru{помогите}, \ru{пожалуйста}}.) What two things is \textbf{\ru{помогите}} made of, and did you own both? (\textbf{\ru{помогать}} and the polite \textbf{-\ru{ите}} — yes, both.) And one look back: which verb sits inside \textbf{\ru{помогать}}, and what are its English cousins? (The verb is \textbf{\ru{мочь}}; the cousins are \emph{may}, \emph{might} and \emph{main}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
